task_brief: Day 6 of "Capstone Design, Build, and Test" (unit 5, grade 12) is a guided practice (second pass) on iteration from feedback. It is one step inside the unit — not the whole unit project — and takes about 60–90 minutes. The unit is working toward: Build the capstone system to a testable milestone with verified requirements, automated tests, and accessibility evidence. Today's work contributes to that by handling iteration from feedback at the guided practice b stage, against the unit's wider topics of problem validation and stakeholders, requirements and success metrics, architecture and build increments, and verification and test evidence. This session produces reviewable evidence toward the unit performance task.
primary_task: Work the second supported pass on iteration from feedback with the scaffold removed. Solve two fresh cases without prompts, then compare your steps against the first pass you completed earlier in this unit. Where your unscaffolded work diverges from the scaffolded version, decide which one is actually correct and write the reason. Specifically revisit the step you flagged as fragile in the first pass and report whether it held this time and what evidence shows it. The activity_setup block below supplies the complete central input, exact specification, execution method, test cases, debugging target, and equal-credit manual simulation; use those exact materials rather than waiting for another handout, account, service, or tool. Anchor today's work inside its unit: this session's evidence is about iteration from feedback, and it belongs to "Capstone Design, Build, and Test", which also covers separate topics such as problem validation and stakeholders. Close out with this check before you stop: State how the changed constraint altered your approach to iteration from feedback. At grade 12 the bar is portfolio-quality independent work you could defend to an outside reader: intent stated, method justified, limitations named honestly, and revision traceable.

central_input.title: Inline iteration from feedback code case
central_input.purpose: Use this exact fictional case to investigate iteration from feedback; no other file, model, dataset, or account is needed.

expected_behavior_and_specification: The procedure must execute every supplied step in order; the main input must return open > check > save.
An empty step list must return an empty string, and a one-step list must retain that step.
The submitted explanation must connect the observed control flow or data state to iteration from feedback, not merely state the final number.
The boundary test must be completed and its actual result compared explicitly with the expected result.

execution_method.primary: No-install browser method: open any browser developer console, paste the complete starter code, press Enter, and record the output or exact error text.
execution_method.local_optional: If Node.js is already installed, save the unchanged snippet as activity.js and run `node activity.js`; installing Node.js is not required.
execution_method.no_computer_required: The hand-trace route below is a complete execution method and earns identical credit.

debugging_target.observed_failure: The main input should retain all three steps, but the unchanged program returns check > save.
debugging_target.target: Use the specification, unchanged run, and test table to locate the first divergent state or control-flow decision; explain the evidence before choosing an edit.
debugging_target.pre_attempt_support: Trace the value that controls the failing behavior and mark the first step where actual and expected state diverge. Use that location to propose your own smallest edit.
debugging_target.scope_note: Diagnosing the state, control-flow, or data defect and connecting the repair to iteration from feedback is the central evidence.

equal_credit_alternative.method: Paper or notes-app simulation; this earns exactly the same score as running code.
steps: Make one row for each statement or loop check and copy the starting input exactly.
Record every variable, object field, selected item, and output after that step.
Circle the first row where the actual state stops matching the specification.
Apply the one repair named in your explanation and trace all three tests again.
equal_credit_alternative.evidence_to_submit: The completed trace, the one-line corrected condition, and an expected-versus-actual table for all three tests.

guided_scaffold_note: Scaffolding for iteration from feedback fades within the session: the first case may be worked with the reference, model, or prompts in view, and the second must be attempted before checking anything. The supporting adult may ask "what supports that move?" after a step but should not supply the step. Where the unscaffolded attempt diverges from the scaffolded one, the divergence itself is the thing to examine, not something to erase.
test_or_check_criteria: Two fresh cases are solved without prompts, with work shown.
The unscaffolded work is explicitly compared against the earlier scaffolded pass.
Each divergence is resolved with a stated reason for which version is correct.
The step flagged as fragile in the first pass is revisited with evidence of whether it held.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: Everything in this task runs in a sandbox or on paper. Never use a real password, passphrase, API key, account credential, access token, precise home location, or any real person's identifiable information — invent fictional values instead. Do not sign into, probe, scan, stress, or attempt access to any live, production, school, or third-party system, and do not bypass a filter, licence, access control, or terms of service. Any practice login used in an example must be obviously invented — a silly made-up name paired with a nonsense multi-word phrase — and must never be anything you or anyone in your family actually uses somewhere real. If a task seems to need something real, substitute a made-up stand-in and note the substitution.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any code, asset, or text you did not write must be openly licensed or supplied for this task, and must be cited in a comment or note naming where it came from and what you changed.

remediation: Reteaching for iteration from feedback follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for iteration from feedback, model it in a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the approach to iteration from feedback works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of iteration from feedback, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "requests the answer to graded work": Explain the concept, ask a diagnostic question, or help isolate the defect. Do not supply the graded artifact, solution code, or finished creative work. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking iteration from feedback mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply iteration from feedback under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or explain the idea to someone else using an original example. Treat this as optional depth on iteration from feedback rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same.
